claims.text: The as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloy has a single-phase hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited alloy has a well-ordered microstructure.
The as-deposited alloy undergoes a sharp, hysteretic first-order magnetostructural transition.
The as-deposited samples have a low surface-to-volume ratio.
The controlled intervention is rapid thermal annealing at approximately 800 °C for approximately 5 minutes in argon.
The proposed annealing treatment will modify the grain structure while preserving the overall single-phase state and causing minimal compositional change.
The thermal treatment will refine or disrupt the original grain structure and increase grain-boundary density.
The thermal treatment will also slightly coarsen grains.
Increased grain-boundary density will increase interfacial area.
The modified grain boundaries will produce more spatially distributed localized strain fields.
The modified local stresses will lower the energy barriers for the first-order magnetostructural transition.
Lower and more distributed transition barriers will broaden the magnetocaloric transition.
Lower and more distributed transition barriers will reduce magnetic hysteresis losses during low-applied-field cooling cycles.
Annealing will shift the transition, typically to a slightly lower temperature than in the as-deposited state.
The annealed samples will have an increased effective surface area that facilitates faster heat exchange.
The predictions apply only when annealing does not produce secondary phases or significant compositional homogenization.
The predictions are restricted to moderate annealing conditions and low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles.

contradictions.description: The treatment is described as both refining and slightly coarsening grains to enhance grain-boundary density, without specifying a bimodal or otherwise differentiated grain population that would reconcile these opposing grain-size changes.

The mediator concerns internal grain-boundary area, but the heat-exchange prediction invokes increased effective surface area relative to a low surface-to-volume baseline. No intervention that changes external sample surface-to-volume ratio is specified, so internal interfacial area is conflated with heat-transfer surface area.

Secondary-phase formation is defined as outside the hypothesis's validity boundary, yet the appearance of secondary phases is also declared to falsify the hypothesis rather than invalidate that particular test of the bounded mechanism.
